raw_response:
I am 39 years old and have been farming our family’s 8 mu of land in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. I only finished primary school, so I do not read many farming books, but I watch what my neighbors do and I remember what worked on my own fields. Last year my wheat gave me about 500 kg per mu and my maize about 550 kg per mu, so I expect about the same this year if the weather holds. This year I will plant winter wheat on all 8 mu in October, and then summer maize right after the wheat harvest in June — that is what almost everyone in our village does, and it is the safest way to make sure we have grain to eat and some to sell.

For wheat, I will rotary till the soil before planting. My neighbor Lao Wang uses improved wheat seeds and gets good yields, so I bought the same kind, about 30 jin per mu. For fertilizer, I will put down roughly 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu before sowing, and then topdress with about 40 jin of urea when the wheat is jointing. That comes to about 17 kg of nitrogen and 11 kg of phosphorus per mu, which is what most people around here use. I irrigate three times for wheat: once at planting, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Water from the well is getting more expensive, but I cannot risk a drought. I spray pesticides about four times — herbicide, insecticide, and fungicide when I see spots on the leaves.

For maize, there is no time to till after wheat harvest; we have to plant within a few days or we miss the season, so I do no-tillage. I plant hybrid maize seeds, about one package per mu. I apply about 80 jin of compound fertilizer at planting, which gives about 11 kg of nitrogen and 3 kg each of phosphorus and potassium per mu. I irrigate twice for maize if the rain does not come. I also spray about four times for pests and weeds. I would rather spend a little extra on fertilizer and pesticide than risk losing half my crop. I do not have much cash saved up, but I know from experience that cutting inputs too much hurts more than it saves.
